quick: IV, titrated to heart rate/symptoms; CAD limit 2-3 mg (0.03-0.04 mg/kg)
Do not withhold life-saving therapy; crosses placenta
Trace amounts in milk after oral intake; data after IV lacking
No specific adjustment stated; not removed by dialysis
Heart rate, PR interval, blood pressure, and symptoms
summary: Atropine sulfate injection is an antimuscarinic (anticholinergic) belladonna alkaloid indicated for temporary blockade of severe or life-threatening muscarinic effects - as an antisialagogue, an antivagal agent, an antidote for organophosphorus or muscarinic mushroom poisoning, and to treat bradyasystolic cardiac arrest. It is given intravenously and titrated to heart rate, PR interval, blood pressure, and symptoms.
indications: Antidote for organophosphorus or muscarinic mushroom poisoning

dosage.d: IV; titrate based on heart rate, PR interval, blood pressure, and symptoms
dosage.n: For IV administration only; single-dose vial, discard unused portion

dosage.d: Restrict total dose to 2-3 mg (max 0.03-0.04 mg/kg)
dosage.n: Limits atropine-induced tachycardia and myocardial oxygen demand

dosage.d: Usual initial dose 0.01 to 0.03 mg/kg IV
dosage.n: Dosing in pediatric populations has not been well studied

admin: Inspect visually for particulate matter and discoloration before use; do not use unless clear and seal intact
Titrate to heart rate, PR interval, blood pressure, and symptoms
Limit total dose to 2-3 mg in coronary artery disease
moa: Atropine is an antimuscarinic agent that competitively (surmountably) antagonizes the muscarinic actions of acetylcholine and other choline esters on structures innervated by postganglionic cholinergic nerves and on smooth muscle responsive to acetylcholine. It blocks peripheral muscarinic receptors of exocrine glands and smooth and cardiac muscle; adequate doses abolish reflex vagal cardiac slowing or asystole. The antagonism can be overcome by raising acetylcholine concentration (e.g. anticholinesterase agents).

relative: Coronary artery disease (limit total dose to avoid tachycardia)
Partial organic pyloric stenosis (may convert to complete obstruction)
Prostatic hypertrophy (risk of complete urinary retention)
Chronic lung disease (inspissation of secretions, viscid plugs)
monitor: Heart rate and rhythm, PR interval, blood pressure

preg: There are risks to the mother and fetus from untreated severe or life-threatening muscarinic events (e.g. acute organophosphate poisoning, symptomatic bradycardia), which are medical emergencies that can be fatal if untreated. Available observational data are insufficient to identify a drug-associated risk of birth defects or miscarriage, and atropine crosses the placenta. Life-sustaining therapy for the pregnant woman should not be withheld because of concerns about effects on the fetus.
lact: Trace amounts of atropine have been reported in human milk after oral intake. There are no data on atropine levels in human milk after intravenous injection, the effects on the breastfed infant, or effects on milk production.
renal: No specific renal dose adjustment is described in the labeling. Atropine is not removed by dialysis.
hepatic: No specific hepatic dose adjustment is described in the labeling.

moderate: Mexiletine - atropine decreases the rate of mexiletine absorption (reversed by adding IV metoclopramide)
interactions.diagnostics: Anticholinergic effects (mydriasis, tachycardia) may confound clinical assessment

serious: Excessive tachycardia increasing myocardial oxygen demand in CAD
rare: Hypersensitivity reactions, especially skin rashes (rarely progressing to exfoliation)
emergency: Anticholinergic toxidrome: hot/dry skin, dilated pupils, delirium, hallucinations, coma
Circulatory collapse and respiratory failure in severe intoxication

monitoring: Clinical symptoms and signs of anticholinergic excess
counsel: This medicine is given by injection in an emergency or supervised setting
Expect dry mouth, blurred vision, light sensitivity, and a faster heart rate
Report difficulty urinating, eye pain or vision changes, or overheating
Tell your clinician about glaucoma, prostate problems, or heart disease
pk: Rapid after IV injection; small doses may transiently slow heart rate before tachycardia
Cardiovascular effects within minutes of IV administration
More potent and prolonged effect on heart, intestine, and bronchial muscle than scopolamine
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); excursions permitted 15-30 C
pearls: Antimuscarinic used for symptomatic bradycardia, bradyasystolic arrest, and organophosphate/muscarinic mushroom poisoning
Small doses may transiently slow the heart before vagolytic tachycardia develops
Limit total dose to 2-3 mg in coronary artery disease to avoid harmful tachycardia
Overdose causes the antimuscarinic toxidrome: hot, dry, flushed skin, mydriasis, delirium ('mad as a hatter, dry as a bone, red as a beet, blind as a bat')
Physostigmine is the specific antidote for severe atropine toxicity; atropine is not dialyzable
missed: Not applicable - atropine sulfate injection is administered by a clinician as needed in acute or emergency situations, not on a fixed self-administered schedule.
overdose: Excessive dosing causes the antimuscarinic toxidrome: palpitations, dilated pupils, difficulty swallowing, hot dry skin, thirst, dizziness, restlessness, tremor, and ataxia; toxic doses cause excitement, hallucinations, delirium, and coma, with circulatory collapse and respiratory failure in severe cases. In children 10 mg or less may be fatal. Treat with a short-acting barbiturate or diazepam for excitement/convulsions; physostigmine by slow IV (1-4 mg adult; 0.5-1 mg pediatric) reverses delirium and coma but may need repeating. Provide artificial respiration with oxygen and cooling measures as needed. Atropine is not removed by dialysis.
